title: The Hulk
full_review:
Angry and larger than life, director Ang Lee's "The Hulk" (Universal) bounds into theaters and fills up the screen, but a problematic script and indulgent length may leave some viewers similarly temperamental.

Inspired by the Marvel Comics character "The Incredible Hulk," the film is initially intriguing as it sets up the story line about mild-mannered and emotionally distant scientist Bruce Banner (Eric Bana). Working diligently with his colleague and former girlfriend, Betty Ross (Jennifer Connelly), Bruce hopes to discover the key to some knotty genetic questions.

One day, in an explosive accident, Bruce is pelted with a normally deadly dose of gamma radiation. But instead of killing him, the radiation has freakishly made him better, stronger and different. Now his repressed anger ignites a monster within, transforming Bruce into his giant, enraged alter ego, the Hulk. And the misunderstood Goliath's rage is only fueled as the military hunts him down to stop his destructive ways and use his genetic mutations as fodder for research.

The film is surprisingly dark as it explores Bruce's repressed memories of his scientist father (scrappy, straggly-haired Nick Nolte, looking like he just got arrested again for drunk driving) and the explosive turning point that left Bruce supposedly orphaned. Lee once again proves that he is a visual master, relating the story through split screens, boxing images to create a comic-book effect. It's as if the viewer is following a comic strip and flipping the pages of a book as one scene dissolves into another.

With lifelike hair and musculature, the computer-generated, emerald-skinned creature moves with agility. Its facial features closely resemble those of Bana's, making the evolution from man to beast more convincing. However, in some scenes where the Hulk leaps across a desert to escape military capture, the digital technology slips into the gimmicky, even producing a few chuckles.

Disappointingly, Lee's steady hand in the first half of the film uncharacteristically shakes in the latter part as the script becomes overwhelmed in its attempt to tie together too many loose plot strands. Two father-child relationships are paralleled on the screen -- Bruce and his father David's, as well as that of Betty and her military father, Gen. Ross (Sam Elliott) -- but neither is satisfactorily explored.

As the viewer begs the question, "Where can this go from here?" the military conquest of the Hulk escalates with computer-generated and choreographed stunts of destruction and mayhem. But it becomes one long big-budget scene slapped onto the next without being very engaging. At various points, the film's last third seems to have reached a conclusion, only to be drawn out again, making the film lose momentum. The writing here becomes sloppy, unraveling as it finally leads up to its anti-climactic ending.

Performances are steady and convincing throughout with the exception of Connelly, who mars an otherwise fine portrayal by turning on the water works each time she wants to convey hurt or frustration.

The humanity of the Hulk is delved into, albeit in a cursory manner, as Betty reminds her general father that underneath the green skin and seething rage lays a broken man grappling with parental death and his new "identity." And Bana's controlled performance elicits compassion and empathy for the character. But even with this and Lee's considerable talent, it is not enough to compensate for the slack script which eventually does in "The Hulk."

Because of sporadic mayhem, violence and destruction, some disturbing images, minimal crass language and profanity and a flash of rear nudity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III --- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
